content: The gingiva, commonly referred to as the gums, is the mucosal tissue that covers the alveolar bone. It is an integral part of the soft tissue lining of the oral cavity, surrounding the teeth and forming a protective seal around them. Unlike the soft tissue linings of the lips and cheeks, the majority of the gingiva is firmly attached to the underlying bone, allowing it to withstand the mechanical forces exerted by food during mastication. Healthy gingiva typically appears coral pink, although it may exhibit physiological pigmentation. Changes in color, such as increased redness, along with swelling (edema) and a heightened tendency to bleed, are indicative of inflammation, often caused by the accumulation of bacterial plaque. The gingiva is anatomically divided into three regions: marginal gingiva, attached gingiva, and interdental gingiva. Marginal Gingiva The marginal gingiva represents the terminal edge of the gingiva that encircles the teeth in a collar-like fashion. In approximately 50% of individuals, it is separated from the adjacent attached gingiva by a shallow linear depression known as the free gingival groove. This region, typically about 1 mm in width, forms the soft tissue wall of the gingival sulcus. The marginal gingiva is supported and stabilized by gingival fibers. Attached Gingiva The attached gingiva is continuous with the marginal gingiva and is characterized by its firm, resilient texture. It is tightly bound to the underlying periosteum of the alveolar bone. On the facial aspect, the attached gingiva extends to the movable alveolar mucosa, from which it is demarcated by the mucogingival junction. Surface stippling may be observed in this region. Interdental Gingiva The interdental gingiva occupies the gingival embrasure, which is the interproximal space beneath the area of tooth contact. Its shape can vary, appearing either pyramidal or as a col shape. Diseases of the Gingiva The gingival cavity serves as a microecosystem, nourished by food debris and saliva, which supports the growth of various microorganisms. Some of these microorganisms can be detrimental to oral health. Poor or inadequate oral hygiene can lead to numerous gingival and periodontal disorders, such as gingivitis or periodontitis (pyorrhea), both of which are major contributors to tooth loss. Recent research has also identified a strong association between anabolic steroid use and gingival enlargement, which often necessitates surgical intervention, such as gingivectomy. Characteristics of Healthy Gingiva Color Healthy gingiva is typically described as coral pink. However, variations in color, such as red, white, or blue, may indicate inflammation (gingivitis) or other pathological conditions. Racial pigmentation can result in darker gingiva, but uniformity of color is more critical than the specific shade. Contour Healthy gingiva exhibits a smooth, scalloped appearance around each tooth. It fills and conforms to the interdental spaces, unlike the swollen gingival papilla seen in gingivitis or the empty interdental embrasures observed in periodontal disease. The gingival margin in healthy gums tapers to a knife-edge thinness, whereas inflamed gums often have a puffy or rolled margin. Texture The texture of healthy gingiva is firm and resistant to movement, often displaying surface stippling. In contrast, unhealthy gingiva is frequently swollen and has a soft, mushy texture. Reaction to Disturbance Healthy gums do not typically react to normal disturbances, such as brushing or periodontal probing. In contrast, unhealthy gums may exhibit bleeding on probing (BOP) and/or purulent exudate (pus).
